title: Financials — How future technology reshapes the sector

slides.title: The technology is not the story. The cost line is.
slides.body: Banks, insurers and asset managers are information processors with a licence. AI attacks the cost of processing and the value of intermediation at the same time. The near-term prize is a lower cost/income ratio; the strategic risk is that payments, advice and underwriting get embedded in someone else's agent interface.

slides.title: What this sector actually sells
slides.body: Revenue comes from spread, fees and float; cost comes from people, legacy systems and regulation. Small changes in either line move returns on equity enormously.
bullets: Net interest income is a spread business: deposit beta and loan pricing matter more than volume.
Fee pools — payments, advisory, asset management, insurance underwriting — carry higher multiples than spread income.
Cost/income ratios of 50–65% leave large absolute cost bases exposed to automation.
Capital and liquidity rules cap leverage, so efficiency and fee mix drive returns.
Trust, distribution and licences are the moat; neither is easily automated.

slides.title: Where the impact lands
slides.body: Two axes matter: how soon the effect reaches reported numbers, and whether it lands on revenue or on cost and capital.

slides.title: The future products in the chain
slides.body: Each stage is a product family that has to exist for the next one to work. This is where the spend lands.

diagram.caption: Deposits and data → risk engines → products → rails → client interface
diagram.note: The interface is where margin migrates. If an assistant owns the customer, the bank becomes a licensed balance-sheet utility behind it.

columns.title: Agentic distribution
columns.body: Customers delegate shopping and admin to assistants, so products must be discoverable and transactable by machine.

columns.title: Tokenised rails
columns.body: Stablecoins and tokenised deposits compress settlement from days to seconds and create new deposit substitutes.

columns.title: Risk automation
columns.body: Underwriting and fraud move from annual review to continuous scoring, with model governance as the constraint.

slides.title: Who gains
bullets: Scaled banks with clean data and the capital to rebuild cores — efficiency gains compound into ROE.
Networks, exchanges and custodians that own rails and can tokenise settlement.
Insurers with proprietary claims data that improves pricing faster than peers.
Asset managers distributing through platforms and agents rather than branches.
Specialist risk and compliance vendors selling into every institution.

slides.title: Who is exposed
bullets: Branch-heavy retail banks with thin fee income and slow core replacement.
Monoline card issuers and processors if agentic rails reduce interchange.
Commission-based advisors whose value is product access rather than advice.
Small insurers with homogeneous underwriting and no data advantage.
Crypto-native intermediaries that lose the compliance arbitrage.

slides.title: What to watch next
slides.body: Signposts are chosen so that each one can falsify part of the thesis within four quarters.
bullets: Deposit beta as tokenised cash substitutes become usable for payments.
Interchange economics in agent-initiated transactions.
Cost/income net of restructuring and vendor spend.
Model inventory disclosed to regulators — a proxy for real deployment.
Quantum migration timelines for core cryptography.
